newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Greenspan warns versus taking risks with inflation.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan warns versus taking risks with inflation.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Tuesday urged central banks not to take risks with inflation and said the best monetary policy was a steady course with the right amount of restraint.
"In the long run inflation is essentially a monetary phenomenon," Greenspan said in a text of a speech at the Catholic University of Leuven in Belgium.
"Accordingly, the best approach (to monetary policy) is to maintain a steady course with an appropriate level of restraint," the U.S. central bank chief added.

The U.S. central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meets next on February 4-5 and is widely expected to opt to hold interest rates steady, despite signs that economic growth speeded up at the end of last year.
Greenspan said that central banks "need to err on the side of caution" in the battle against inflation and warned policymakers in general not to forget the lessons of the stagflation of the 1970's.
"The recent record on inflation reduction in industrial countries has been impressive," he said. "We should take care, however, that our recent success not make us complacent."
Greenspan credited much of the success in the fight against inflation to the emergence of a consensus among governments that inflation does not create jobs.
"But to sustain good inflation performance, we need to understand the other factors that lie behind our recent success," he said.
They include increased competition, especially from emerging market economies in Asia and Latin America, that has made it more difficult for companies in many countries to raise prices, he said.
Workers worried about losing their jobs have also helped hold down inflation by not pushing for big wage increases, accroding to the Fed Chairman.
"Workers at present, to a greater extent than usual, trade aspirations for higher levels of earnings for job security," Greenspan said.
In setting policy, central banks must balance the risk of printing too much money and fanning inflation with the risk of printing too little and stifling the economy, he said.
But the central goal of money policy "should and will" remain the achievement of price stability, Greenspan said.

The problem, though, is pinning down exactly what that means. "As the century draws to a close, the simple notion of price has turned decidely ambiguous," Greenspan said. "What is the price of a unit of software or a legal opinion?"
He said it was "crucial" that statisticians develop new techniques of measuring prices. The Fed Chairman has been one of those who have argued that the U.S. consumer price index overstates inflation.
Central banks must also take account of the impact that their policies have on the rest of the world, Greenspan said. That is particularly true of countries like the United States.

"Countries whose currencies are widely used internationally, like the United States, have a special responsibility to provide an anchor of stability for themselves and the rest of the world," the Fed chief said.
He said was encouraged by the progress regulators have made in tackling the risks posed by the settlement of hundreds of billions of dollars each day in the world currency market.
While technological advances in some respects have raised the risks of more rapid and widespread disruptions to financial markets, Greenspan said that they have benefits as well.
"Because the evolution of new technologies takes time, I suspect that we have tended to exaggerate the negative effects of information and data processing technologies on financial markets," he said.
New technologies, for example, make it easier for banks and other financial institutions to measure and manage risk.
While central banks need to minimise market disruptions from bank failures and the like, they should only use that power rarely, Greenspan said.
"Central banks ... provide what essentially amounts to catastrophic financial insurance coverage," he said. "Such a public subsidy should be reserved for only the rarest of disasters.
